title: The Universe in Her Son's Mouth
story:
In Gokula, Yasoda sat nursing her baby, the small son of Nanda and herself. There is no hour more ordinary in a mother's day than the hour when she feeds her child, and this was such an hour: the child on her lap, nearly done with his milk, his drinking slowing. His name was Krishna, and she was looking down at him the way any mother looks at the small face she loves, with its sleepy, contented smile. The afternoon was warm and still around them; dust motes turned slowly in a shaft of light by the door, and from the lane came women's voices and the lowing of cattle.

And the child yawned.

It was only a yawn, the kind every tired baby makes. But as his mouth opened, Yasoda looked into it, and instead of the pink of a child's gums she saw the sky. She saw the wide sky, and the earth spread out beneath it, and the heavens beyond, and the hosts of stars turning in their courses, and the four directions, and the sun and the moon and fire and wind and the great oceans — and every living thing that moves or stands still. The whole universe lay arranged inside the open mouth of the baby she was holding.

She saw all of it, suddenly and at once, and her body began to shake. Her limbs trembled and her breath caught in her throat, and she trembled the way a leaf trembles in a strong wind, for she understood, in that instant, that the small mouth before her opened onto everything. Her arms tightened around him, and still she could not look away.

It lasted no longer than a yawn lasts. Then the moment passed, and Krishna was only a baby again — warm and drowsy against her, his mouth once more too small for anything but a kiss. He could not yet speak a word. He offered no explanation and asked for none. He had only yawned, and let her look.

The walls of the room came back around her, and with them the ordinary sounds of the village — a cow lowing, a neighbor calling, the afternoon light lying across the floor. Yasoda sat a long while without moving, the child asleep in her arms, and she said nothing at all. What she had seen had been given to her without a word, for no reason but that she was his mother and happened to be looking. She had held the sky and the sea and everything that lives inside the open mouth of her own son, and she carried what she had seen the way one carries a thing too large to speak of: quietly, and always.
reflection: The vision is given to a mother in the most domestic of moments, while she is nursing, and it is not sought or asked for. The infinite does not interrupt her love; it shows itself through the very child she is holding.
hero_scene: Yasoda, the child on her lap, stares into his yawning mouth and sees the whole universe within it, the sky and oceans and sun and moon and stars, while she trembles.
visual_elements: Yasoda with the infant on her lap
the sky, earth, oceans, sun, moon and stars within it
